title: 20 minutes from disaster: Jet carrying 300 holidaymakers from Cancun declares 'mayday' over Birmingham after nearly running out of fuel in 100mph winds
text:
An plane that transported almost 300 tourists occurred at 20 minutes from the disaster after almost running out of the air.
The Boeing 787-8, flying from Cancun in Mexico, had to arrive at Manchester airport during the winds of 100 mph Storm Pia in December 2023.
Hooking to Earth, the pilot was informed that he was behind seven planes that expected the conditions to be facilitated so that they could land safely.
Air traffic controllers could not give it an estimated time to land, so the 62 -year -old commander chose to deviate to the East Midlands airport.
But East Midlands said he could not cope with a plane of his size, so he was redirected to Birmingham.
The extreme winds forced him to abort the first landing attempt. Directing to have a second chance, a ‘Mayday’ declared because the plane was worked dangerously under fuel.
At that stage, the plane, which was sent in a diversion of 28 miles despite declaring a fuel emergency, could not fly to another airport.
A security report issued today by the air accident investigation branch (AAIB) said that the plane, which transported 291 passengers and ten crew, landed with only 1,250 kg of fuel.

With the plane burning 60.5 kg per minute, it would probably have run out of fuel in 20 minutes, just enough to land if it had to go for the second time due to strong winds.
According to safety rules, it should have landed with fuel of 1911 kg.
Tui passenger jet, Tom173 flight number, left Cancun at 5.50 pm local time on December 20, 2023, for a night flight to Manchester.
The crew was informed of strong winds in England, but believed that they would dissipate around 6 am, with the plane due to the earth at 7.35 am
However, they chose to load additional 984 kg of fuel as caution, equivalent to around 15 minutes of flight.
First they contacted Manchester Air Traffic Control at 7.18 am, where they were told to roll on the airport, behind seven planes they already expected. At that time, the plane was 5,500 kg of fuel.
The controller told the pilot that it was not possible to provide a landing time since the delay was unknown. The pilot surrounded his airport several times before trying to deviate.
The wind speed was around 32 mph, with bursts up to 47 mph.
At 7.28 am, the pilot called East Midlands Radar informing that they may need to divert there, but three minutes later they were told “we cannot accept their size plane.”

At 7.41 am, six minutes after its scheduled landing time, the diversion of the plane was accepted to Birmingham airport, but only 4,100 kg of fuel had left. This is the equivalent of approximately one hour.
In the first contact with Radar, the pilot said: “We will have a minimum fuel.”
At 8.05 am, the plane cleared to land and began to descend, but had to leave the landing at 240 feet on the ground due to the wind speeds, which were burst at 43 mph.
During the climb to 4,000 feet, at 8.08 am, the crew contacted the radar of Birmingham saying ‘Tom173 Mayday Mayday Mayday, Tom173 Mayday Fuel’.
Air traffic controllers send the plane on a route to 25 miles south of the airport before placing them behind a second plane, more than double duplicating the distance to 53 miles, which cost them a total of 1,450 kg of fuel.
The 28 miles added reduced the fuel reserve of the plane in another 400 kg.
The plane finally landed in Birmingham at 8.26 am with 1,250 kg of fuel, equivalent to about 20 minutes of flight time.
The flight was supposed to last eight hours and 45 minutes, but instead it lasted nine hours and 36 minutes.
AAIB’s report on the incident found that Birmingham’s air traffic controller should have prioritized the flight before.
The investigation concluded that the controller faced a “complex and high workload scene” that resulted in the opportunity to prioritize Tom173 while repositioning a Wizz Air plane that was lost.
This resulted in Tom173 flying an extended track even though he had declared an emergency of fuel, according to the report.
The AAIB Report concluded: ‘While allowing the contingencies required by the regulations, the operators seek to minimize the transport of fuel necessary for the flight, because the penalty for fuel burns transports an excess of fuel.
‘However, the crew identified a threat of strong winds and the potential for delays on arrival at Manchester airport.
‘Believing incorrectly that the winds would dissipate from 0600 hours, the commander requested an additional fuel, equivalent to approximately 15 additional fuel minutes. Given the weights of the airplanes, the crew had the option of loading significantly more fuel.
‘The consistent reduction in the fuel that remained had the effect of reducing the options available to achieve a safe landing, if the aircraft had found a gank in the second approach.
‘The serious incident was the result of strong winds that generated difficult conditions at the time of the arrival of the United Kingdom flight.
“Security measures have been taken to clarify the process to determine and communicate the capacity of the deviation airport, and for the prioritization of airplanes that have declared an emergency.”
